title: 'They're feeling aggrieved': Ex-Ryder Cup captain laments pros hurt by LIV's demise
article_text:
When LIV Golf ended in early November, it would have been easy to brand LIV’s players as the biggest losers in the ordeal.

But Paul McGinley sees things very differently.

As dozens of former LIV pros sign on with the DP World Tour for 2027, the former European Ryder Cup captain and current TV analyst thinks the current DP World Tour pros have the most to lose.

In a recent appearance on Sky Sports, McGinley lamented the “difficult scenario” those players face in their careers with LIV pros returning to Europe following pro golf’s “ugly” civil war.

LIV’s unceremonious demise in bankruptcy court left its remaining players with a problem. With doors to the PGA Tour shut tight (for now), they had nowhere to play in 2027.

On Tuesday, the DP World Tour announced that LIV’s biggest star, two-time major winner Bryson DeChambeau, would join its ranks next season. Nine other ex-LIV pros, Dustin Johnson among them, signed deals with the DP World Tour, too.

Suddenly, the DP World Tour’s 2027 membership had gained enormous firepower (especially when considering Jon Rahm’s earlier commitment to the tour).

While LIV’s stars joining the DP World Tour is great for European fans and the tour’s coffers, it’s potentially bad news for the tour’s existing players. They will now have to compete with dozens of accomplished LIV players for prize money and playing time.

When the news of LIV pros returning to the DP World Tour broke, McGinley joined Sky Sports to express his sympathy for those European players getting a raw deal after LIV’s demise.

The biggest problem current DP World Tour players face, McGinley argued, is with earning tour status for 2028.

“The guys I feel sorry for are the guys, not so much next year in 2027 on the DP World Tour, it’s 2028, because you’ve got 30 really world-class players coming back to play on the DP World Tour next year from LIV, and they’re probably going to take 20 or 30 of the 100 cards that are available,” McGinley said this week. “So there’s really 20 or 30 less spots for the current players to play for next year in terms of keeping their status for 2028.”

He continued by admitting he understood why current rank-and-file DP World Tour pros would be “aggrieved” by the situation they find themselves in.

“So that’s going to be a difficult scenario for them. And, you know, they didn’t get the riches that the guys who went to LIV did. So, you know, I can understand why they’re feeling aggrieved,” McGinley said.

McGinley isn’t the only one who holds that opinion. Two of the DP World Tour players negatively impacted by a wave of LIV pros joining up next year have made similar arguments recently.

Six-time DP World Tour winner Joost Luiten argued that the tour’s leaders should make it more difficult for former LIV players to join its ranks.

“[The DP World Tour] should make it harder for guys to come back. Four years ago they didn’t give a s— about the DP World Tour,” Luiten told Today’s Golfer. “They made a decision to go after the money. And now all of a sudden, the money is gone and they want to come back and act like nothing happened. I don’t think that’s right.”

Then, earlier this month, two-time PGA Tour winner Erik van Rooyen, who splits his time on the DP World Tour, argued that since LIV players “gave the finger to the Tour,” they should be forced to “go back to Q-school” rather than be given sweetheart deals for accelerated PGA Tour returns.

But while McGinley feels for players negatively impacted by LIV players’ reintegration into mainstream pro golf, he also argued that there were “no real winners” from the “ugly” civil war that tore pro golf apart. The primary mission now is to try to “put the pieces back together,” even if that means some players get left behind.

“There’s no real winners in this whole scenario, you know? There’s not a clear-cut winner in this scenario. It’s been pretty ugly for golf in the last two or three years, and now it’s time to put the pieces back together,” McGinley said on Sky Sports. “And starting next year, having the LIV guys back playing in Europe, is the start of trying to put this game back together and relationships back together.”

title: Tiger Woods Set for PGA Tour Comeback at December's Hero World Challenge
article_text:
Fifteen-time Major champion Tiger Woods will make his return to competitive golf this December at the Hero World Challenge in the Bahamas.

The 50-year-old icon has been sidelined from official tournament play since missing the cut at the 2024 Open Championship at Royal Troon. His last appearance at the marquee Caribbean tournament came in 2023, where he placed 18th.

Although Woods took part in the TGL and teased an appearance at the Masters last April, his schedule was derailed by an automobile accident in Florida and an extensive rehabilitation stint at a specialized clinic in Switzerland. The strict secrecy surrounding his physical condition had cast doubt on whether the legendary golfer would tee it up on Tour again.

Tournament organizers confirmed Woods' participation on Tuesday after he was awarded one of three sponsor exemptions for the limited-field event, which benefits his charitable foundation. Fellow PGA Tour veterans Rickie Fowler and Gary Woodland received the remaining two invites.

Currently unranked in the Official World Golf Ranking (OWGR) and having completed just four full 72-hole events across the past six seasons, Woods was notably absent from the initial field announcement in October.

This upcoming start marks Woods' 19th career appearance at the Hero World Challenge, a tournament he has won five times (2001, 2004, 2006, 2007, and 2011). Chasing a sixth victory will be a formidable test, with the elite field featuring six of the world's top 10 players.

title: Ludvig Aberg Leads String Of RSM Classic Withdrawals
article_text:
Former champion Ludvig Aberg leads a host of withdrawals from the RSM Classic in Georgia - the final event of the PGA Tour season.

The RSM Classic is the last event in the FedExCup Fall season where the final PGA Tour cards for next year will be on the line.

The Swede claimed his maiden PGA Tour victory at the 2023 RSM Classic but after also missing it last year he won't be in the field this time around due to back injury.

The 27-year-old said on social media that he tweaked his back in the build-up to the tournament and although an MRI showed no serious damage he's decided to play it safe.

Aberg finished fourth on the FedExCup this season but did not manage a tournament victory - he's not played since the Open de Espana as he decided to skip the DP World Tour Play-Offs in the Middle East.

He was due to make his return at the Seaside and Plantation Courses at Sea Island Resort in St. Simons Island, Georgia, before the back problem struck.

"I tweaked my back a few days ago and while the MRI showed nothing I felt it was best to play it safe and give it some time," said Aberg.

Aberg is one of eight players from the origianl RSM Classic field to withdraw, with Daniel Berger and Sudarshan Yellamaraju joined by Emilio Gonzales, William Mouw, K.H. Lee, Kevin Yu and Frankie Capan III.

Brooks Koepka headlines the field now with young guns and recent winners Jackson Koivun and Blades Brown lining up alongside the likes of Tony Finau, Marco Penge, Rasmus Hojgaard, Keegan Bradley and Brian Harman.

Paul Higham is a sports journalist with over 20 years of experience in covering most major sporting events for both Sky Sports and BBC Sport. He is currently freelance and covers the golf majors on the BBC Sport website. Highlights over the years include covering that epic Monday finish in the Ryder Cup at Celtic Manor and watching Rory McIlroy produce one of the most dominant Major wins at the 2011 US Open at Congressional. He also writes betting previews and still feels strangely proud of backing Danny Willett when he won the Masters in 2016 - Willett also praised his putting stroke during a media event before the Open at Hoylake. Favourite interviews he's conducted have been with McIlroy, Paul McGinley, Thomas Bjorn, Rickie Fowler and the enigma that is Victor Dubuisson. A big fan of watching any golf from any tour, sadly he spends more time writing about golf than playing these days with two young children, and as a big fair weather golfer claims playing in shorts is worth at least five shots. Being from Liverpool he loves the likes of Hoylake, Birkdale and the stretch of tracks along England's Golf Coast, but would say his favourite courses played are Kingsbarns and Portrush.

title: Inside 2031 Ryder Cup host Camiral and how England can stage 2035 edition
article_text:
England has not hosted the Ryder Cup since 2002, but 2031 host Camiral offers insight into a potential winning bid.

Laying on a photobiomodulation bed across the corridor from a cryogenic chamber, having spent an hour in an oxygen chamber, is not your usual Tuesday. Camiral Luxury Resort, on the outskirts of Spanish city Girona, is opulent, exclusive and is evermore catering to sports teams such as Arsenal and England Rugby.

Its sports recovery programme is an “experience designed to relieve muscle fatigue, reduce inflammation and restore mobility” but doesn’t come cheap, at £200 per day on top of usual resort fees. Having experienced 100 per cent oxygen – and its eerie silence – and the low-level laser therapy photobiomodulation provides, it is difficult – if not a little amusing – to imagine the likes of Tyrrell Hatton doing the same.

But the Brit might, because Camiral Luxury Resort will host the 2031 Ryder Cup. Having initially been built for the 1997 edition, which was eventually moved to Real Club Valderrama in the south of Spain, Catalunya is set to experience the inter-continental tournament for the first time.

It is the continuation of a recent trend – 2027 host Adare Manor aside – in Europe of purpose-built courses getting the biggest competition in team golf after Le Golf National in Paris and Marco Simone in Rome. It also means the wait for a Ryder Cup in England, a first since the Belfry in 2002, will go on until at least 2035.

So why has Camiral got it so right, and how can England learn from the luxury modernisation of golf?

“What the Spanish, French and Italians have done very well is the great collaboration with the wider tourism industry,” YGT, formerly Your Golf Travel, chief Keith Francis tells City AM. “If you look at Camiral, the logo is on the bags and the towel that you would buy in the shop for 2031. It’s Camiral, it’s Girona, it’s Costa Brava, it’s Catalunya, it’s Barcelona and, by its very nature, they’ve got everybody on board throughout the journey.

“If we are able to work collaboratively with federations, councils and governments, that’s where [others have] got it right. To host the Ryder Cup now is a whole infrastructure, whether it be the capacity around the course or the railway line that gets you there.”

Hulton Park near Bolton is planning on a £240m golf resort to host the “biggest ever” Ryder Cup, while Royal County Golf Club in Newcastle is submitting plans for significant upgrades. The Belfry, too, has opened new luxury facilities. What Camiral has, however, is the space to expand – it has two courses and may merge them, or build a new one, for the Ryder Cup – and the high-end offering many English courses cannot offer.

“What a great story that would be if we could host a Ryder Cup at a links golf course,” adds Francis. “The key point is about it being somewhere where people can play and enjoy and go on holiday – that’s a great selling point. And there is a story there of legacy; you’ve got Rome and Italy not being really that well known for golf – a little bit like Paris – and they did the best job of having a legacy of people travelling and an uplift after it.

“People like something different, they want to play the marquee golf courses as a starting point, and then they want to hear what is the next best thing. They like to be able to brag to their friends about golf courses and they want to feel that they’re still getting value as well. Green fees are expensive now.

“It’s got to be our turn because it has moved around. If I was a betting man I’d say it’s got to be around a city somewhere, whether that be London or Manchester.”

There’s something divine about quietly dining out on succulent lamb overlooking Catalan fairways (having been zapped by miniature lasers) knowing hundreds of thousands will pack the space around the dotted trees in five years’ time and roar on Europe. It is an example of the present and future of golf, and somewhere any aspirational English course should inspect if they’re to return the Ryder Cup to these shores.

title: Nelly Korda Eyes LPGA Earnings Record at $11M Season Finale
article_text:
NAPLES, Fla. — Nelly Korda can pass Annika Sörenstam on the LPGA’s career money list this week at the CME Group Tour Championship with a finish of 6th place or better.

But the No. 1-ranked women’s golfer in the world is trying to block that out of her mind at the $11 million LPGA season finale, which will award $4 million to its winner—the largest individual prize in women’s golf.

“I feel like when you start focusing on that mentally, I just don’t really like that,” Korda said Wednesday at her pre-tournament press conference. “I like to be a kid mentally on the golf course and think about it in a way where I do this because I love to do this, not because it’s a job.”

But Korda isn’t the only one closing in on Sörenstam, who has been atop the LPGA money list for 25 years. Lydia Ko, a 2024 LPGA Hall of Fame inductee, can also pass Sörenstam this week with a fifth-place finish or better.

While Korda has been as financially successful as anyone in women’s golf, she said the prize money is actually “the last thing I look at. Sometimes it’s like a pinch-me moment that I get to play this game for a living, that I get to live a really great life doing what I love and not really looking at that aspect of the game.”

Korda leads the LPGA’s 2026 money list with $6.31 million in on-course earnings this season, boosted by a $2.5 million winner’s check at the U.S. Women’s Open, and $1.35 million for her Chevron Championship victory. She earned a combined $4.59 million at the five major championships this year.

Korda said she hasn’t tuned in to a WTGL match yet in the league’s inaugural season, which debuted Nov. 8.

“I have been really busy, so I have not been able to catch it, but I’m sure I will,” Korda said. “They started when I was coming back last week competing, so I’ve been a little busy.”

Korda previously criticized WTGL’s women’s-only format, calling it a “huge and unbelievable miss” that LPGA players weren’t competing alongside the men.

Fellow LPGA star Rose Zhang, a member of WTGL’s New York Golf Club, told FOS last month that Korda joining the league would be “very good for the game. She’s a headline name, so it would obviously bring a lot of attention to WTGL.”

Despite Korda’s absence, LPGA commissioner Craig Kessler said Wednesday he has been impressed with “the way our players are showing up,” pointing to the likes of Michelle Wie West coming out of retirement, in addition to several up-and-coming players. “The energy it’s creating is phenomenal, and the personalities, as we’ve talked about, are really starting to show up in a cool way,” Kessler said.

title: DP World Tour 2027: Fewer cards, LIV ban and returning stars
article_text:
The DP World Tour has set its membership categories for the 2027 season, and the changes are significant. A total of 199 exempt members from 29 countries make up Categories 1 to 18. The number of full exempt cards falls from 110 to 100. Only the top 100 on the 2026 Race to Dubai Rankings keep full playing privileges, and players ranked 101 to 110 move into the conditional Category 18.

The pathways onto the tour are also narrower. At the Qualifying School Final Stage, the top 15 and ties now earn Category 18 membership, down from the top 20 and ties. Graduates from the HotelPlanner Tour, the tour's feeder circuit, fall from 20 to 15. Taken together, the changes are expected to leave about 20 fewer card holders in 2027.

The tour says the aim is to give existing members "more-balanced playing opportunities." It expects the season ahead to be "one of the most keenly contested campaigns in our 55-year history."

Category 1 has 22 players and covers recent major champions and Race to Dubai winners. It includes Rory McIlroy, who won his eighth Race to Dubai title in 2026, along with Jon Rahm, Shane Lowry, Matt Fitzpatrick and Justin Rose. Bob MacIntyre is confirmed in Category 2, which is reserved for Rolex Series winners.

The headline addition is Bryson DeChambeau. The American takes up full DP World Tour membership in Category 1 thanks to his 2024 US Open victory. He is scheduled to make his debut as a member at the Hero Dubai Desert Classic in January 2027 and is expected to play at least 12 DP World Tour events.

Nine other players who left for LIV Golf have signed invitation-only agreements with the tour. They are major champions Dustin Johnson, Cameron Smith and Bubba Watson, together with Joaquin Niemann, Lucas Herbert, Carlos Ortiz, Abraham Ancer, Thomas Pieters and Michael LaSasso. Their agreements start at the Bapco Energies Bahrain Championship in 2027 and do not include access to Rolex Series events.

The deals follow LIV Golf's decision to wind down after the 2026 season. Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund put more than $5 billion into the league over five years, then announced in April 2026 that the funding would stop.

The tour has also closed the door on dual membership. Players can no longer hold LIV Golf and DP World Tour membership at the same time in 2027 and must choose one circuit. Players who held conditional dual status through the 2026 season faced a commitment deadline of November 16, 2026.

"Players need to make a choice," said DP World Tour CEO Guy Kinnings. "As we have said for many years, we have rules and regulations which are there to protect our tour and which our members must all abide by."

Kinnings also welcomed the returning players: "For us, it's the prospect of having incredible talent joining our tour, which already is laden with talent." The tour called its decision a "pragmatic approach to this unique and unprecedented situation," made "always with the best interests of our entire membership at the forefront."

The ban could also matter for the Ryder Cup. European players who have been with LIV, such as Tyrrell Hatton and Tom McKibbin, may now feel more pressure to commit to the DP World Tour if they want to stay eligible for the team.

The 2027 schedule has 42 events in 24 countries, and the BMW International Open remains the tour's stop in Germany. With fewer cards on offer and more star power in the fields, every place will be hard won next season.

title: The 14 first-time winners on the 2026 Race to Dubai
article_text:
Across the 2026 season on the DP World Tour, we saw 14 first-time winners, with those players accounting for 16 victories in total.

From David Puig in the season-opener to Joe Dean on home soil, via mutiple winners and veterans breaking through, the DP World Tour's first-time winner's class of 2026 has a bit of everything.

Let's get to know them all a little better.

Ever since he made the cut at his home open as a 19-year-old amateur in 2021, the Spaniard has been on many people's radar and he has quietly gone from strength to strength ever since.

He made the cut on his Major debut at the 2023 U.S. Open and the following year registered back-to-back top fives on the Back 9 at the Open de España and Alfred Dunhill Links Championship.

Two more top fives followed in the Middle East early in 2025 and, now becoming a Club de Campo Villa de Madrid specialist, Puig once again finished in the top ten at his home event.

His first 14 events had shown stellar potential and in his 15th at November's BMW Australian PGA Championship it all came to fruition as he followed in the footsteps of the great Seve Ballesteros to become just the second Spaniard to win the Kirkwood Cup.

The 24-year-old then registered two top tens in Dubai and a top 20 at the US PGA Championship represents his best Major finish to date.

The Dane's breakout victory felt like it was a long time coming, which is astonishing considering it occurred in just his 42nd start.

The 2024 Road to Mallorca champion was winless on the 2025 Race to Dubai, yet he very much announced himself as a player to watch at the top of leaderboards, notching 11 top‑ten finishes before breaking through in the early stages of this season.

Neergaard‑Petersen spent 2025 establishing himself as one of the most polished rookies on the DP World Tour. His consistency kept him in the mix at several big events, and one of his standout moments came at the DP World Tour Championship, where he earned a place in the final group alongside Rory McIlroy. Though his late push - picking up five shots in his final five holes - saw him come up just short of winning the title, the composure he showed under Sunday pressure underlined just how quickly he was adapting to elite company.

His performance at Royal Melbourne at the Crown Australian Open then showcased the full breadth of his development as he held off Major winner and home hero Cam Smith to take a one-shot victory.

Since then he has made his Masters debut, while he finished in the top ten at The Open.

Schaper’s rise from promising South African talent to genuine DP World Tour star saw him finally reach his potential in impressive style on the Opening Swing.

He collected nine top tens from 27 starts on the 2025 season as he truly established himself on Tour but the 2026 campaign has seen him take things to another level.

After years of knocking on the door, he finally claimed a maiden victory at the 2026 Alfred Dunhill Championship, producing a chip‑in birdie at the 16th and an eagle at the first extra hole to defeat defending champion Shaun Norris.

That victory unlocked something deeper: a surge of belief that carried him to another play-off triumph just a week later at the AfrAsia Bank Mauritius Open, where he holed out for eagle on the second extra hole to secure back‑to‑back wins and close out the year as one of the Tour’s most in‑form players.

2026 has brought a best Rolex Series finish wth a top five in Dubai and debuts at the US PGA Championship, U.S. Open and Open Championship and went on to secure dual membership with the PGA TOUR after finishing a career best eighth on the Race to Dubai.

They say that if at first you don't succeed, try try again and that is particularly apt for Schott.

Despite being just 24 at the time of his win, it feels like the German has been around a while and that is because it is fair to say he has taken the scenic route to the top.

Coming from the same Düsseldorfer Golf Club as fellow DP World Tour star and good friend Marcel Siem, the six-time DP World Tour winner acted as a mentor to the teenage Schott and even had him caddie for him on Tour.

Schott turned professional in 2021 after some regional amateur success and won his first professional event on the ProGolf Tour at the FaberExposize Gelpenberg Open that same year.

His second victory came on the HotelPlanner Tour at the Frederikshavn Challenge - Presented by HESSEL as he finished ninth on the 2022 Road to Mallorca to earn his way onto the DP World Tour.

He lost his card in his rookie season but gained it straight back as he won Qualifying School Final Stage and while he once again failed to keep his playing privileges in 2024, two top tens in limited starts in 2025 saw him secure his card for 2026.

And he took full advantage in February, defeating Calum Hill and Patrick Reed in a play-off to win the Bapco Energies Bahrain Championship for his first DP World Tour title.

He has since claimed one further top five at the Volvo China Open and another top ten at the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship, eventually finishing his year at 27th on the Race to Dubai.

title: McGinley Warns Of Crowded DP World Tour Field In 2028
article_text:
Paul McGinley, the former European Ryder Cup captain, has issued a stark warning about the future of the DP World Tour. He believes the return of 30 world-class players from the LIV Golf circuit will squeeze out current members by the 2028 season. The former captain spoke to Sky Sports on Tuesday about the math involved in this massive shift. After Bryson DeChambeau and others secured their spots, he told the outlet that "there are no winners in this whole scenario"

Bryson DeChambeau is the most high-profile name to return, earning Category 1 status through his 2022 and 2024 U.S. Open wins. This status lets him play in any event he chooses. These deals exclude Rolex Series events, per reports. The tour says these spots will "add value to those tournaments" while trying to keep things fair for existing members.

McGinley focused his concern on the year 2028 rather than the immediate 2027 season. He explained that the flood of talent will consume a huge chunk of available playing cards. "Because you've got 30 really world-class players coming back to play on the DP World Tour next year from LIV, and they're probably going to take 20 or 30 of the 100 cards that are available," McGinley said. This leaves significantly fewer spots for players who stayed loyal during the split.

LIV defectors received massive financial guarantees that the regulars on tour never received. The few remaining cards now face the toughest competition from them. McGinley noted that the real pain will be felt when these returning stars try to keep their status for the following year. The situation creates a brutal environment for players who did not leave the game for the breakaway league.

Rory McIlroy sees the return of DeChambeau as a positive step for the sport overall. The Northern Irishman believes the attention DeChambeau commands brings more eyes to the game. "I think a name like Bryson DeChambeau and everything he brings with him, good and bad, he brings eyeballs, which is a good thing for tournaments," McIlroy said, according to Yahoo Sports. While McGinley worries about the cards, McIlroy focuses on the boost in visibility for fans and sponsors.

Kinnings believes the plan will benefit the tour as a whole by ensuring top players remain visible for fans. The tour plans to launch its 2027 season next week with the BMW Australian PGA Championship.

DeChambeau quoted Arnold Palmer to make his point about humility. "Arnold Palmer said no player is bigger than the game, and I want to acknowledge that, along the way, I've said some things that didn't help," DeChambeau said, according to Yahoo Sports. This shift in tone was preceded by backlash over his conduct at The Open in July.

Dominating the DP World Tour to earn a PGA Tour card back for 2028 is his clear plan. Reaching this goal requires him to secure a top 10 finish in the Race to Dubai standings. DeChambeau's first step is the Nedbank Golf Challenge in South Africa next month. His 2027 campaign is anticipated to launch with The Hero Dubai Desert Classic in January.

title: Brooks Koepka: American labels his 2026 PGA Tour season a 'disappointment' and targets 2027 Ryder Cup spot
article_text:
Brooks Koepka has dubbed his 2026 season a "a disappointment" but insists he is hungry to secure a spot on Team USA's 2027 Ryder Cup squad.

The American returned to the PGA Tour via the one-time-only Returning Member Program in January following his LIV Golf exit at the end of 2025, a decision he said he was "beyond happy with".

After being welcomed back to the tour with open arms, Koepka made his return at the Farmers Insurance Open in February. He'd go on to make 16 starts on the PGA Tour this year but would miss the cut at five events and record only one top-10 finish.

- DeChambeau joins DP World Tour: What does it mean for men's golf?

- What golf is live on Sky Sports and when? Full TV listings

Koepka, who was not selected as one of Keegan Bradley's captain's picks for the 2025 Ryder Cup and was also omitted from Brandt Snedeker's President's Cup team in 2026, hopes to raise his game and earn a spot in the roster for next year's Ryder Cup.

"Adare Manor is a big goal of mine," Koepka said. "But this year has just been a little bit of a disappointment, so I know I need to pick it up a little bit.

"It's something I don't enjoy, sitting back watching the Presidents Cup.

"I know I've only played in one [2017], a lot of those [omissions are due to] injuries. But those team events are a lot of fun, I really enjoy them.

"Getting to be around the guys and representing your country is pretty cool.

"So, anytime you can do that, or you have the opportunity to, and you're not able to go play, it kind of infuriates me sitting on the sidelines."

The 36-year-old has featured in four Ryder Cup's in the past, notably helping Team USA to victory in at Hazletine in 2016 and Whistling Straits in 2020.

He boasts an overall individual record of 7-6-2.

Koepka was the lone player to elect to sign up to the PGA Tour's Returning Member Program, with Jon Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau and Cameron Smith all snubbing the deal, instead choosing to remain at LIV Golf in 2026.

However, following the dissolution of the formerly Saudi-backed breakaway league, Rahm, DeChambeau and Smith have all elected to rejoin the DP World Tour for the 2027 season, along with multiple other former LIV Golf players.

Koepka, meanwhile, was asked ahead of this week's RSM Classic whether he felt back at home after returning to the PGA Tour, replying: "Yeah, I felt very at peace with coming back.

"The reception was fantastic from all the players, caddies, just everybody on tour.

"I think I kept a good relationship with everybody even when I left.

"I think that played probably a huge part in that.

"Everybody was really receptive. I loved the conversations that I've had just throughout the year, just guys asking what was going on, thought process and how things went and the decisions made to get back here.

"Everything was great. I'm beyond happy with my decision."

title: DP World Tour Offers Star Invites To LIV Defectors
article_text:
The professional golf world faces a new reality as the DP World Tour moves to fill its fields with high-profile names from the collapsing LIV Golf circuit. Nine players who left their original tours to join the Saudi-backed league have been offered a path back through sponsor invitations, a move that prioritizes star power over traditional meritocratic rankings. This shift comes as LIV Golf winds down through bankruptcy proceedings, leaving many players in limbo while tour officials scramble to stabilize the game's ecosystem.

According to Rediff, European Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings acknowledged the rapid shift in the sport, stating, "There has been significant change in the landscape of men's professional golf over the past 12 months." The tour is now offering these invitations without the hefty appearance fees that characterized the LIV era, aiming to inject excitement into lower-ranked events. This strategy targets specific stops that need a boost in star power, ensuring fields remain competitive even if depleted of top-tier members. According to Ronan MacNamara from Irish Golfer Magazine, up to 34 individuals previously associated with LIV are set to retain DP World Tour status in the coming year, a figure appearing inflated due to the former league's hostile maneuvers against the tour.

The tour has secured the returns of major stars like Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton, and Bryson DeChambeau, which officials view as a positive step for the DP World Tour. CODE Sports reports that Cameron Smith has also been offered a career lifeline following the collapse of LIV Golf, though the terms come with specific conditions. Dustin Johnson, Bubba Watson, Cameron Smith, and Joaquin Niemann are among those receiving a "specific number" of tournament invitations to beef up events where they play. These players, who previously defected with a seemingly endless supply of Saudi cash, now face a different reality as that funding disappears. The arrangement allows these high-profile names to compete without taking spots from lower-ranked players who earned their way through the system. Kinnings emphasized the pragmatic nature of this approach, noting that the tour has always kept the best interests of its entire membership at the forefront of its mind.

Longtime supporters of the European tour have raised concerns about the implications of this policy. The tour previously sent 10 players to the PGA Tour annually, yet now it risks banning PGA Tour players with greater profiles than those it is losing. The idea behind the sponsor invitations is to place these stars in European tour stops that need help, giving those tournaments a boost without taking away spots from fields that were already depleted. This creates a unique situation where players who never contributed to the tour are now being welcomed back with open arms. The move promises to be exciting for European golf fans and head honchos at the Tour, but it leaves rank-and-file members questioning the fairness of the system.

As the DP World Tour integrates these former LIV players, the relationship with the PGA Tour remains a critical factor. With the PGA Tour's partnership with Europe ending next year, talks continue to alter and prolong the agreement. PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp confirmed on Wednesday evening that discussions are productive, stating, "both entities have a mutual desire to extend and modify our partnership." The modification will likely include how many PGA Tour cards are offered to leading players in Europe, but it is most certain to be fewer than before. This reduction in card availability adds another layer of complexity to the integration of these high-profile returnees.

Kinnings believes the upcoming season will be highly competitive despite these changes. He noted that with the return of major champions and the inclusion of former LIV stars, "Our 2027 season is set to be one of the most keenly contested campaigns in our 55-year history." The inclusion of players like Rahm and DeChambeau adds significant weight to the tour's schedule. However, the financial stability of these players remains uncertain as the LIV league dissolves.

The next major development will be the finalization of the 2027 season schedule and the specific allocation of cards for European players. The PGA Tour and DP World Tour must resolve their partnership terms before the season begins. The outcome of these negotiations will determine how many European players can access the PGA Tour and how the remaining spots are distributed.

title: CME Group Tour Championship: Field, format, prize money as Nelly Korda, Charley Hull, Lottie Woad battle for win at LPGA finale
article_text:
Who will be crowned the LPGA Tour’s Race to the CME Globe Champion? Who can stop Nelly Korda from winning? Can Brits Charley Hull and Lottie Woad claim victory? We get you up to speed ahead of this week’s LPGA Tour 2026 season finale, live on Sky Sports.

What is the CME Group Tour Championship?

The CME Group Tour Championship is the final event in the LPGA Tour's season-long points race.

Throughout 2026, players have competed in the LPGA Tour's points competition, the Race to CME Globe.

- What golf is live on Sky Sports and when? Full TV listings

The top 60 players on the Race to CME Globe Points List are invited to feature at this weekend's event and the player who wins the 2026 CME Group Tour Championship will be crowned the Race to CME Globe champion.

Where is the CME Group Tour Championship held?

The tournament is held at the Tiburon Golf Club at the Ritz-Carlton Golf Resort in Naples, Florida.

The course has hosted the tournament since 2013.

It is the second time in consecutive years that Korda has arrived at the CME Group Tour Championship sitting at the top of the Race to CME Globe standings.

The American has already been crowned the Rolex Player of the Year, with three events to spare, but has never won the Race to CME Group Tour Championship. A first title this week would see her qualify for the LPGA Hall of Fame.

Standing in her way is a field of the LPGA Tour's best players, including two-time CME Group Tour Championship winner Jeeno Thitikul, who arrives in Florida having won four times on the LPGA Tour this season.

Miyu Yamashita, who has three wins on the LPGA Tour in 2026, enjoyed a strong finish to her season, winning twice while placing inside the top 10 three times in her last six events.

Haeran Ryu, who clinched back-to-back majors at The Amundi Evian Championship and the KPMG Women's PGA Championship, also comes into this event off the back of a fine vein of form, finishing tied-second and tied-third in her last two starts.

Hull clinched the first LPGA Tour title of her career at this event back in 2016, so she certainly knows how to win at Tiburon Golf Club.

It's been a great year for Hull, who won the Solheim Cup with Team Europe in September and placed inside the top 10 at five LPGA Tour events. She'll no doubt want to end the season in style with a win.

Woad is the only other English player in the field. She too has enjoyed an excellent year, winning the Kroger Queen City Championship in May and finishing tied-ninth at last week's The ANNIKA, marking her seventh top-10 finish of the season.

A total prize purse of £8.33m ($11m) is up for grabs, with the winner set to take home a £3.03m ($4m) cheque, the biggest cash prize in the history of women's golf.

The runner-up is also set to receive £757,423 ($1m).

What other end-of-season awards are up for grabs?

The LPGA Tour will also award the golfer with the lowest scoring average across the 2026 season with The Vare Trophy.

While Korda holds the lowest average score for the year, she has not played enough rounds to qualify for the award, meaning Yamashita, who has a scoring average of 69.50 and Thitikul, who follows her at 69.87, will battle it out to win The Vare Trophy.

How to watch the CME Group Tour Championship?

Sky Sports will be showing all four rounds of the CME Group Tour Championship live.

The first two rounds of the tournament will be shown live on Sky Sports Mix from 7pm on Thursday and Friday, with the action also live from 8pm on both days.

The third round coverage starts at 6pm on Saturday on both Sky Sports Mix and Sky Sports Golf, while Sunday's action is also live from 6pm on Sky Sports Golf and Sky Sports+.

Coverage of the final round will begin at 6pm on Sky Sports+.

title: ‘I’m pretty appalled’: DP World Tour star blasts chiefs over LIV invites
article_text:
The two-time winner accuses the Tour of a “massive miscalculation” and warns that invitations for former LIV golfers risk undermining the circuit’s integrity.

Eddie Pepperell has accused the DP World Tour of a “massive miscalculation” over invitations for former LIV golfers, saying he is “pretty appalled” by a policy he believes risks undermining the integrity of the circuit.

The Englishman described the situation as “borderline unethical” and questioned why players who failed to earn a card at Q School should be handed opportunities ahead of existing members.

On Tuesday, the DP World Tour confirmed invitation agreements with nine former LIV players: Dustin Johnson, Cameron Smith, Bubba Watson, Abraham Ancer, Lucas Herbert, Michael La Sasso, Joaquin Niemann, Carlos Ortiz and Thomas Pieters.

The deals begin at the Bahrain Championship and cover designated tournaments, excluding Rolex Series events. The number of invitations for each player has not been disclosed.

Speaking on this week’s The Chipping Forecast podcast with broadcasters Andrew Cotter and Iain Carter, Pepperell said the issue had changed how he felt about the Tour he has spent his career supporting.

“Let’s not forget, because it’s so easy to forget given how quickly things can shift, these [players] are coming from a tour that, as Guy Kinnings just described, was set to destroy our own. And yet they’re still being handed opportunities. It’s not the same as just giving an invite to Rory McIlroy when he first came out, or another up and coming star who hasn’t participated in a league that had ulterior motives and a deterious impact on the DP World Tour.

“I’ve really been grappling with this, and it’s been a bit of a stressful two weeks in my mind, because it does start to bring in ethical considerations, because this is borderline unethical. You can have different views on the strategic, commercial things as you see it panning out, but I do think there’s also an ethical component to this and – and I want to show some restraint – I’m pretty appalled and it has massively impacted the way I feel towards the Tour. I predicted that would happen a few weeks ago and it has happened.”

Other former LIV players have qualified through existing membership categories. Bryson DeChambeau, for example, has joined under Category 1 through his 2024 US Open victory, while former Legion XIII Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton, who won the tour’s final two events in Abu Dhabi and Dubai respectively, never resigned their memberships and have settled their fines.

Pepperell questioned the need to offer starts to players including Michael La Sasso and Charles Howell III – players who’ve never previously shown a desire to play in Europe. La Sasso won LIV’s final tournament in Indianapolis but failed to progress beyond the Second Stage of DP World Tour Q School.

He nevertheless has invitations to the Australian PGA Championship and Mauritius Open, giving him starts in two of the first four events of the wraparound season.

The former NCAA champion gave up a Masters place to join LIV earlier this year. His only DP World Tour appearance came at October’s Dunhill Links Championship, where he missed the cut.

By contrast, former LIV players Josele Ballester and Byeong Hun An secured their playing rights through Q School.

La Sasso, Ortiz, Pieters and Caleb Surratt are all listed under professional tournament invitations for next week’s Australian PGA, which opens the 2027 season at The Lakes in Sydney on November 26.

At the time of writing, Pepperell is first reserve. He had already booked flights, expecting to be in the field, but said he would not make the long trip without a confirmed place in the field.

The Australian PGA invitations are separate from the DP World Tour’s nine agreements starting in Bahrain. Pepperell acknowledged that tours, promoters and sponsors can each control invitations, leaving the public unable to tell who has awarded a particular place.

But he argued that the Tour’s stated intention to invite former LIV players had opened a “can of worms” over how those decisions would be perceived.

The 35-year-old also recalled why the Legends Category was created during Keith Pelley’s time as chief executive, arguing that those places should be treated like invitations.

“They’re there for commercial reasons. And I say that knowing that because I was on the committee in 2018 when the category was created and Keith Pelley specifically came to us and said ‘if Miguel Angel Jiminez wants to play a tournament, we need him there.’”

He said the combination of invitations and the Tour’s Legends Category could result in 20 to 25 places in a 140-player field going to golfers whose eligibility was not based on current or previous-season performance.

“My pushback would be, constructively, you need to redress that balance.”

He contrasted that with the PGA Tour’s incoming Championship Series: approximately 120-player fields without sponsor exemptions from 2028.

He warned that the Tour risked the “WWE-ification” of sport.

“It’s not to say that’s not a successful product; it’s just an unserious product. And if what you’re trying to sell is top-level sport, which is what the DP World Tour supposedly is, you have to be very careful about that balance because you undermine the integrity of it.”

He also challenged the argument that returning LIV players would attract bigger crowds and television audiences.

“To play devil’s advocate with that point, why then was LIV Golf not a raging success? What LIV Golf proved was that players who’ve had these careers had far less impact than we thought they did. Why? Because they were playing under an umbrella and what they represented was fundamentally an athema to what most sporting fans respect when it comes to sport, and that’s history, integrity, performance and genuine competition… and a competitive pyramid.”

title: Bryson DeChambeau 2027 DP World Tour schedule: What it could look like around the majors
article_text:
Bryson DeChambeau's decision to sign up for the DP World Tour in 2027 has got the golf world talking.

Following the collapse of LIV Golf, the two-time U.S. Open champion is barred from playing on the PGA Tour for at least 12 months, unless the American circuit decides to take a softer approach and welcome back players from the renegade league.

Given the most recent sentiments expressed by new PGA Tour commissioner Brian Rolapp on the topic, the prospect of seeing DeChambeau feature in 2027 seems unlikely.

Rather than stepping back from tournament golf to focus on his booming social media empire, DeChambeau has decided to take up an exemption on the DP World Tour.

His U.S. Open triumph in 2024, when he beat Rory McIlroy by a shot, affords him status in the top tier, meaning he is free to pick and choose his own schedule.

You can expect to see him target the lucrative Rolex Series events and tournaments around the four men's majors.

GolfMagic has decided to take a look at when and where DeChambeau might play.

We already know where DeChambeau's journey begins.

He has committed to Gary Player's Nedbank Golf Challenge at Sun City in South Africa over 3-6 December, giving him an immediate chance to bank crucial Race to Dubai points.

DeChambeau is unlikely to play the Mauritius Open the following week, and therefore it is likely he will begin the calendar year by playing in the Dubai Desert Classic over 21-24 January.

He has the option of staying in the region and playing in the Bahrain Championship a week later.

With no PGA Tour events available to keep his game sharp ahead of the Masters in April, DeChambeau will need competitive reps in March.

The Hero Indian Open, played over 18-21 March at DLF Golf and Country Club, will surely appeal.

DeChambeau made no secret of how much he enjoyed his first trip to India last January, when he played the International Series event on the Asian Tour.

Once the green jacket has been decided, there are a couple of tournaments that might catch his eye.

Last October, the DP World Tour announced the return of a historic national open. The Deutsche Bank Singapore Open, at Sentosa Golf Club, will be contested over 15-18 April.

Given that it falls a week after The Masters, DeChambeau may choose to skip it.

The Volvo China Open (22-25 April) may appeal, too.

The European Swing beckons in May, and there will be no shortage of opportunities for DeChambeau to get in some competitive reps ahead of the PGA Championship in Texas (20-23 May) and July's Open Championship at St Andrews.

The Catalunya Championship in Spain slots neatly onto the calendar two weeks prior to the PGA Championship.

After the second men's major of the year, there are several more opportunities for DeChambeau ahead of the U.S. Open at Pebble Beach.

The BMW International Open in Germany, Soudal Open in Belgium and KLM Open in the Netherlands will all be contested before DeChambeau attempts to win another major.

DeChambeau is desperate to win The Open and has made it clear how much he wants to tame links golf.

Before the champion golfer of the year is decided, DeChambeau could look at competing at the Italian Open in late June or even the Irish Open at the K Club at the beginning of July.

It seems likely, though, that DeChambeau will tee it up at the Scottish Open (8-11 July), a week before the 155th Open is contested at the home of golf.

After the major season is complete, and if DeChambeau is in contention for one of those coveted top-10 PGA Tour cards, September through November will be decisive.

The DP World Tour's Back 9 kicks off over 19-22 August with the British Masters, hosted by Sir Nick Faldo, but given the history between the pair, it doesn't seem likely that DeChambeau will be travelling to the Belfry.

The French Open (9-12 September) stands out, but it is being played a week before the 2027 Ryder Cup.

It's also a shame that the DP World Tour's flagship event, the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth, is being staged a week after Europe's tussle with the United States at Adare Manor.

So, it is more likely that DeChambeau will be eyeing up the Spanish Open (7-10 October), India Championship (14-17 October) and Hong Kong Open (21-24 October) before the DP World Tour's playoffs begin in November.
