You can also take a look at the full DP World Tour schedule at the bottom of this page.

title: Aggreko renewed as Official Supporter of the 2027 Ryder Cup
article_text:
Aggreko will continue its long-standing relationship with the Ryder Cup next autumn at Adare Manor in Limerick, Ireland.

Aggreko has renewed its partnership with the Ryder Cup by becoming an Official Supporter of the 2027 match in Ireland. The sustainable energy provider will supply power and HVAC across the event, including the broadcast compound, hospitality facilities and wider event operations.

The Ryder Cup is one of golf’s most iconic tournaments, with an expected attendance of 250,000 spectators across the week. Next year sees the 100th anniversary of the Ryder Cup, and will be Aggreko’s sixth year supporting the contest, celebrating its return to Ireland after 20 years.

A team of over 50 people will work at Adare Manor in Limerick, Ireland, arriving on site in March 2027 to begin the initial power set-up. Aggreko’s scope includes lighting design and support, site-wide temporary power provisions and temporary HVAC, providing over 2,000 lights and 172km of cabling across a 40-week project period.

The brand has been transforming temporary energy since 1962, from powering the world's largest sporting and entertainment events to bringing critical energy to remote communities across the world. Aggreko will bring its extensive experience and expertise to support the Ryder Cup once again in 2027, delivering efficient temporary energy solutions through considered design, detailed planning, economical delivery and sustainability focused fuel management.

“We are proud to continue supporting the Ryder Cup in 2027, as one of the highlights of the golfing calendar,” said Jono Rose, Managing Director, Aggreko Event Services. “Every major sporting event has unique demands. Aggreko combines proven expertise with innovative energy solutions to meet these challenges, helping to reduce emissions while ensuring the Ryder Cup is delivered seamlessly.”

“We’re delighted to continue working with Aggreko, whose best-in-class service and industry knowledge are second to none,” said Kit Gartrell, Ryder Cup Event Delivery Director at the European Tour Group. “Every event offers new opportunities to refine our energy supply and respond to the demands of the course. With Aggreko’s expertise, we are confident that our operations team and partners can deliver the most famous event in golf seamlessly.”

title: Bryson DeChambeau announces new project after US Open champ joined DP World Tour following LIV Golf collapse
article_text:
BRYSON DECHAMBEAU has been a busy boy since LIV Golf went kaput.

The Saudi-backed rebel golf league’s collapse threatened to leave the two-time major winner in the lurch.

But this week he committed to playing on the DP World Tour in 2027.

And he also has his fingers in a number of other pies.

DeChambeau’s YouTube channel has over 3million subscribers, and he posts multiple long-form videos every month.

Another exciting project, which was announced last week, will see DeChambeau design a brand new championship golf course in his home town.

‘The Orchard’ will be a state-of-the-art 18-hole facility in Clovis, California, featuring an on-site farmer’s market and “numerous other community amenities”.

DeChambeau wrote in a signed statement: “There is a deep responsibility to give back to the region that provided us with so much.

“To fulfill that vision, we are proud to introduce ‘The Orchard’.

“The course and practice facilities will be designed by my team and will be the first of many fully procured DeChambeau Designs.

“We anticipate approval within 18 months, with some amenities such as a driving range coming sooner.

“It’s time to make a better future for our next generation.

“It is our hope that this will be a place where everyone in the world can come and enjoy the fruits of our labor here in the Central Valley.”

DeChambeau was one of LIV’s poster boys before Saudi pulled their funding, sending the league into a deathspin.

The PGA Tour – where DeChambeau played before joining LIV – typically enforces a one-year ban dating back to a player’s final LIV appearance.

But he is now guaranteed entry into any DP World Tour event, beginning with Gary Player’s Nedbank Golf Challenge, which the American has already announced he will play in next month.

title: No regrets: Smylie outlines post-LIV Golf future
article_text:
Elvis Smylie has no regrets after leaving the LIV Golf building, as the Australian attempts to parlay a medical exemption into full-time European status.

- A rib injury forced the 2024 Australian PGA champion to the sidelines for almost three months after a $6 million solo win with LIV Golf.

- A medical exemption will give him key DP World Tour opportunities next year after LIV Golf announced it would wind down operations.

- Victory at next week's Australian PGA Championship or next month's Australian Open could fast-track his full-time status.

The 2024 Australian PGA champion was a $6 million solo winner on debut as part of Cameron Smith's all-Aussie LIV Golf team earlier this year.

However, as he balanced starts on both the rebel tour and Europe's DP World Tour, a rib injury became worse and eventually forced him onto the sidelines for almost three months.

The breakaway LIV Golf tour nosedived at the same time and announced this month it would begin winding down operations after losing key players and the funding needed to continue operating.

It left Smylie floundering for status and grinding in Spain's final round of European tour qualification, where he missed a spot despite shooting 22-under through six rounds.

However, ahead of this week's Queensland PGA Championship at Brisbane's Nudgee layout, the 24-year-old confirmed a medical exemption would offer him key opportunities next year.

"Eleven weeks out was hard to take and there were a lot of big tournaments I missed," he said.

"But the [DP World Tour] events I missed this year, I'll play next year, hopefully re-rank and get out there fulltime.

"It [LIV Golf] was great while it lasted and I took my opportunities.

"Financially it was great ... it meant I can have my team travel with me more often and with the injury, I learnt it's vital you have the right people around you.

"What I'm ready for is stability and consistency."

Smylie can fast-track his full-time status with victory at the Australian PGA Championship at The Lakes in Sydney next week, or at the Australian Open at Melbourne's Kingston Heath next month.

An Open victory also comes with a Masters invite, while a top-three finish earns a spot at the Open Championship.

Smith, Lucas Herbert and a host of LIV Golf's biggest names have also been granted various levels of access to the next European Tour season, bulking up an already quality field.

"It's going to make the tour better and the players are going to be working harder and harder," Smylie said.

Smylie will fancy his chances at Nudgee, where he was a Pennants-playing member as a child.

However, in his way is defending champion Cameron John, who punched his DP World Tour ticket with six rounds of 68 or better to finish third in Spain at 33-under.

title: The PGA Tour is simplifying, but rules governance remains complicated
article_text:
The most powerful word Brian Rolapp, the CEO of the PGA Tour, used late Monday afternoon while talking to reporters in a remote press conference was simple. Well, two longer forms of it, more precisely: simplify and simplification. The occasion was the announcement of the concluding work, conducted over the past 18 months, by the Tour’s Future Competition Committee, chaired by Tiger Woods, who was not present for this confab powered by . . . Microsoft Teams, the preferred video conferencing service of the PGA Tour.

“We have seen the success of PGA Tour University across the PGA Tour system and it will now serve as the basis of eligibility on the Korn Ferry Tour,” Rolapp said at the start, reading from prepared remarks. “From the outset, we said we wanted to simplify the model and ensure there was a clear path for top performers at every stage of their career.”

I’m drawn to the word, because the world is complicated and golf is simple, or it should be. What is golf but an ancient overland game requiring its players to bat a small ball toward and into an annoyingly small hole with specified equipment, playing, all the while, your ball as it lies, the first and most essential rule that coexists with various others?

The play conducted by PGA Tour players is essentially simple. It aggregates the adventures of a group of men who are “chasing a little white ball” (per Rory McIlroy, repeatedly). The players count strokes. They count their own shots played, while counting the shots played by others, too. A two-way check. (Can you imagine tax returns if any of us could audit anybody we wished?) In theory, any and all golfers, male or female or otherwise, can play their way onto the PGA Tour. All you have to do is shoot the scores. In a manner of speaking and in a far more specific context, Rolapp was saying that very thing. He was summarizing the work of the Future Competition Committee.

“Before I open up to questions, I will briefly address LIV because I suspect it might come up today. We have heard from our fans and we know that they want the best players playing together and we share that view. I have said that from day one when I took the job I am interested in doing whatever makes the PGA Tour better. That said, as we have a membership organization, we have rules, and as I shared before, they exist to ensure fairness and competitive balance. Rules matter and they will be enforced.”

Any competition committee at any level can run with that sentence.

I used to play in a fall golf event where you couldn’t make more than a triple bogey on any hole. It was a rule, a generous one, you could say, aimed at speeding up the pace of play for the field while keeping hope alive for individual players.

The LPGA recently announced new rules for 2027 aimed at improving the pace of play. When it’s your turn, you have to play your shot within 60 seconds. The clock is ticking. Six seconds too long will cost you a shot. Sixteen seconds too long will cost you two. Rules matter and they will be enforced. You can only hope that is a statement that applies across the game, wherever it is played.

The rules that govern play on the PGA Tour are not decided by its Future Competition Committee. But all golf competitions, including this week’s event at Sea Island, in the Georgia Lowcountry and hosted by a local, Davis Love III, start with its rules. One of the greatest insights I ever got about how to view the role of the rules in golf came from Davis, years ago. We were talking about how TV viewers could call in possible rules violations they observed. “It’s not like you’re trying to get away with anything,” Love said, “so why wouldn’t you want all the help you can to turn in the most accurate scorecard possible?” Flawless logic.

The first page of the rulebook instructs golfers to play the course as you find it and to play your ball as it lies. Bryson DeChambeau was penalized at the British Open at Royal Birkdale this year because he didn’t do that. In a manner of speaking, a viewer picked up on that: a rules official watching on TV. The official saw DeChambeau taking heavy-footed steps in the rough behind his ball in the rough of the fifth hole in the second round, thereby improving his lie. I couldn’t see it, watching the TV replays, but people with far more experience than I, including Rory McIlroy watching in real time, could. The Open’s competition committee gave DeChambeau two shots. He had failed to play his ball from its original lie.

Earlier this month, McIlroy received a two-shot penalty in the first round of the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship, a DP World Tour event, for violating the same rule in a different way. On the 12th hole, with the flange of his sand wedge, he pressed too firmly into the grass behind his ball. The rule permits you to press “lightly,” letting a player rest the club with its actual weight but not apply his or her own force. In layman’s terms, you can’t shove your clubhead behind the ball.

In my casual golf, I almost never see anybody violate this rule, in spirit or in fact. Jack Nicklaus never did, because he always hovered his club over the ball when it was in a grassy lie. Watching a replay of the McIlroy situation, I could not readily see an issue. A rules official, watching on TV, could — or eventually could. A small tuft of grass that had been immediately behind McIlroy’s ball no longer was. He had changed his lie by being too aggressive while preparing to play his shot.

title: Report: Former LIV Golf star weighing shock one-year sabbatical after DP World Tour absence
article_text:
Former LIV Golf star Sebastian Munoz is reportedly considering taking a one-year break from professional golf, with the Colombian's future becoming an interesting talking point after missing out on a series of DP World Tour invites for 2027.

Munoz, 33, joined LIV Golf in 2023 and represented Joaquin Niemann's Torque GC throughout his time on the breakaway circuit. He enjoyed a significant moment in his LIV career last year, claiming his maiden individual victory at Indianapolis.

However, his name was notably absent from a group of nine former LIV players who have agreed to receive invitations to selected DP World Tour events next season. That absence does not necessarily mean Munoz was denied an opportunity, with it remaining unclear whether he was interested in pursuing the arrangement in the first place.

Nevertheless, Handicap 54 suggested on X that the Colombian could now be contemplating an extended absence from professional golf.

"The situation regarding the Colombian golfer Sebastián Muñoz is worth watching closely," posted Handicap 54, which is often among the first to break golf news across Latin America.

"It was notable that he was not included in the agreements with the DP World Tour, and it is my understanding that he has been considering taking a one-year sabbatical (this is not confirmed, but I know it is an option he has weighed)."

Munoz was not the only recognisable former LIV Golf player missing from the latest DP World Tour arrangements.

American veteran Charles Howell III was also notably absent, despite his name having previously been linked with a potential route onto the European circuit for the 2027 season.

His inclusion in those discussions had suggested that a move towards the DP World Tour could be an option, but that anticipated pathway has seemingly not materialised.

Howell had been representing Bryson DeChambeau's Crushers GC on LIV Golf. He won his sole LIV event at Mayakoba in 2023, and he won three times on the PGA Tour, with his first way back in 2002 and last in 2018.

The nine players who have agreed to receive DP World Tour invitations for the 2027 season include Dustin Johnson, Cameron Smith, Bubba Watson, Abraham Ancer, Lucas Herbert, Michael La Sasso, Joaquin Niemann, Carlos Ortiz and Thomas Pieters.

Johnson, Watson and Smith are the most notable names, having collectively won five major titles between them, while Munoz's former Torque GC captain Niemann established himself as one of LIV Golf's most successful players, collecting nine individual titles and approximately $85.4 million in official prize money. Munoz's former Torque GC teammate Ancer also made the list.

Importantly, the agreements do not provide the nine players with full DP World Tour membership, unlike former LIV stars Bryson DeChambeau, Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton and Patrick Reed, for example. Instead, they relate to invites for select tournaments, beginning with the Bapco Energies Bahrain Championship in January 2027.

The $10 million Rolex Series events are excluded, with designated tournaments identified for each player.

A separate group of nine former LIV players, including Sergio Garcia, Lee Westwood, Ian Poulter, Louis Oosthuizen and Martin Kaymer, also secured DP World Tour membership through the career money list.

Handicap 54 also used Munoz's situation to highlight wider concerns about the changing professional golf landscape and its potential impact on players from Latin America.

The account believes the end of PGA Tour Americas following the 2027 season, alongside concerns about the strength of Korn Ferry Tour fields, could leave important regional tournaments struggling to attract competitive players.

Those concerns come after the PGA Tour confirmed the final details of its new developmental structure, which will come into effect in 2028.

The Korn Ferry Tour will remain the principal pathway to the PGA Tour, while a new PGA Tour Challenger Series will provide another competitive tier.

The top 20 players on the Korn Ferry Tour will earn membership on the Challenger Series for the following season, while the top 90 players on the latter circuit will qualify for its season-ending championship.

PGA Tour Americas, meanwhile, will stage its final season in 2027 before being replaced by a network of affiliated events operated alongside third-party partners.

Although the PGA Tour believes the changes will create a more connected development system, Handicap 54 fears that players from Latin America could face greater financial and logistical obstacles when attempting to establish themselves professionally.

"The Latin American golf market appears to be collapsing, and no one seems to be doing anything to revive it," the account added.

A potential sabbatical would represent a significant development for a player who has previously established himself at the highest levels of both the PGA Tour and LIV Golf.

Before joining the breakaway league in 2023, Munoz claimed his only PGA Tour title at the 2019 Sanderson Farms Championship, defeating Sungjae Im in a playoff.

He subsequently represented the International Team at the 2022 Presidents Cup, collecting an impressive 2.5 points from three matches despite his side eventually losing 17.5-12.5 at Quail Hollow Club.

Munoz also earned a silver medal for Colombia at the 2023 Pan American Games, finishing just one stroke behind Mexico's Abraham Ancer, who was also a member of Torque GC.

For now, there has been no official confirmation that Munoz intends to step away from professional golf.

However, as Handicap 54's report suggests, with his future plans uncertain and the professional landscape continuing to evolve, the Colombian's next move will certainly be worth monitoring.

title: Columbia University Publishes Economic Impact Study of the 2025 Ryder Cup
article_text:
Graduate students in Columbia University's Master of Science in Sports Management program have completed an independent economic impact study of the 2025 Ryder Cup at Bethpage Black, delivering their findings to 2025 Ryder Cup executive staff. The project was conducted as a supervised research course led by Brian Connolly, founder and managing principal of Victus Advisors, during the fall 2025 semester.

“The Ryder Cup’s influence extends far beyond the golf course. As golf’s premier team event, it brings thousands of attendees from around the world and generates meaningful economic impact for local communities, businesses and the broader region. Having Columbia University independently assess that impact provided tremendous value to the PGA of America. We were particularly impressed by the rigor of the students’ work and appreciated the opportunity to give the next generation of sports industry leaders a firsthand look at what it takes to plan and deliver a global sporting event. Their work also provided valuable insight into the Ryder Cup’s impact on the host community." - David Charles, Senior Director of Championships, PGA of America

“We are thrilled to have authored the economic impact report. This is yet another expression of the program's scholar-practitioner model that prepares our students with the practical skills needed to achieve success in the sports industry. Brian did a fantastic job leading our students through the process. We very much appreciate working with the PGA of America and their terrific staff, who allowed us the independence to conduct an analysis that yielded some amazing results for New York State.” - Scott Rosner, Program Director and Professor of Professional Practice, M.S. in Sports Management Program, Columbia University School of Professional Studies

“This project gave Columbia students a rare opportunity to contribute to a real-world analysis tied to one of the most legendary events in golf. I was impressed by the way they combined analytical rigor with practical problem-solving, especially given the scale and visibility of the Ryder Cup. The quality and defensibility of their economic impact analysis is a strong example of what the next generation of sports business professionals can bring to the industry.” - Brian Connolly, Lecturer, M.S. in Sports Management Program, Columbia University School of Professional Studies, Founder and Managing Principal, Victus Advisors

The Supervised Research Project is a course in Columbia's Master of Science in Sports Management program that places graduate students in a consulting role on an industry engagement. Most recently, at the behest of the PGA of America, the program produced an independent economic impact analysis of the 2025 Ryder Cup, held September 26-28, 2025, at Bethpage Black Golf Course in Farmingdale, New York.

Over the course of the semester, students worked through the full lifecycle of an economic and fiscal impact engagement, including client scoping and information requests, a site tour and kickoff meeting with the PGA of America, survey planning and distribution, and on-site event support at Bethpage Black. They then processed survey data, analyzed gross and net-new direct spending, estimated fiscal impacts, considered intangible benefits, provided a progress update to the client, prepared the final report, and presented their findings to PGA leadership.

The independent economic impact analysis conducted by Columbia University estimated that the 2025 Ryder Cup at Bethpage Black generated approximately $622.5 million in gross direct spending, including approximately $398.5 million in net new direct spending within New York State after accounting for displacement effects. The analysis combined ticket purchaser survey data (collected from 1,472 Ryder Cup attendees) with operational and event-related information, including ticket sales, hospitality, merchandise, sponsorship, staffing, taxes, attendee demographics, travel behavior and media reach. The findings showed substantial spending both at the event and across the broader visitor economy, including lodging, food and beverage, transportation and retail activity. Out-of-state visitors generated an estimated 193,946 hotel room nights, while total sales tax revenue to New York State was estimated at approximately $34.7 million. In addition to its direct economic and fiscal impacts, the study found that the Ryder Cup elevated New York’s global profile through significant tourism activity, international visitation, and media exposure.

title: The 8 things you should actually care about from PGA Tour changes
article_text:
Maybe Tiger Woods was waiting for his work at the PGA Tour to finish before making plans to return to pro golf.

On Tuesday morning, the 15-time major champ announced his latest competitive return at next month’s Hero World Challenge. On Monday night, though, the PGA Tour group that Woods has led for the last two years, the Future Competitions Committee, announced its final sweep of radical changes to the world of pro golf.

The latest changes outlined by golf’s “FCC” are the final infinity stone in a constellation of tweaks announced over the last six months, and answer the final critical questions surrounding how the new system will actually, y’know, work.

If you’re a golf fan with a normal sense of boundaries, you’re probably at least a little burned out by the idea of change. The PGA Tour has been changing in some way for what feels like half a decade now, and in the last six months, it has held three separate press conferences to promote a new array of sweeping adjustments to the regular way of life.

But what do those press conferences actually mean? And what do you, the average fan, actually need to know? Let’s run through the 8 biggest takeaways from the new way of life below.

The big headline here is that these changes are a really big deal, and they’re also final. Starting in 2028, every single golf tournament on golf’s largest pro tour will look and feel measurably different than it does today. The players, the tournaments, the field sizes, the field invites, the sponsors and, yes, even the castoffs will look different under the new system.

So, what’s the big picture? The PGA Tour will split into two tours: the “Championship Series” and the “Challenger Series.” The Championship Series will feature only the top 110 players on Tour; the Challenger Series will feature everybody else. The Championship Series will feature most of the PGA Tour events you go out of your way to watch (Torrey Pines, Arnold Palmer; Memorial; Doral); the Challenger Series will feature the best of the rest. The Championship Series will have a $20 million purse per event; the Challenger Series will pay out … less than that.

Yep, get your weird friend who drinks beers at 9 a.m. on a Saturday on the line, because the PGA Tour is experimenting with European soccer-style promotion and relegation beginning in 2028.

Under the new system, the top 90 players will stay on the Championship Series each year, while the bottom 20 will be relegated to the Challenger Series and replaced with the top-20 finishers from the lower series.

The Tour postseason is the biggest “structural” change under the new system. Forget the old system, where a steadily dwindling field of players eventually competed to be named Tour Champion. Under the new system, the BMW Championship will be the final stroke play event of the season and will feature the top 90 players from the Championship Series competing for the title of “season-long champion.”

After the BMW Championship, the top 32 finishers will fill the seeding for the new “Tour Championship,” a two-week, bracket-style match play event modeled after the World Cup. Allegedly, the new Tour Championship will also be played at epic golf courses not typically seen in pro golf, but the exact machinations of that setup are still TBA.

For years, when people asked me what “kind of status” a player had on the PGA Tour, I usually shrugged. The truth was that there were tons of ways to earn a promotion to the big tour, and the pathway for most players was different. Some came up through “PGA Tour U,” some came through “Special Temporary Membership,” and some came up through something called a “battlefield” promotion (which allegedly had nothing to do with actual combat experience).

Now, that whole system is out the window, and replaced by a single, unified ranking system based entirely on performance. Think of it as one long ladder: every player below the PGA Tour level — Korn Ferry Tour members, Q-School grads, college stars, and pros grinding through a new network of Tour-affiliated events — goes on the same list. Where you sit on that list decides which fields you get into. Climb past a threshold, and you’re bumped straight up to the new Challenger Series. This was the biggest change announced Monday afternoon by PGA Tour leadership.

“From the outset, we said we wanted to simplify the model and ensure there was a clear path for top performers at every stage of their career,” Tour commissioner Brian Rolapp said in a press conference. “To that end, we will develop a new unified priority ranking that puts every player in the developmental system on one list.”

Golf fans who actually understand the current FedEx Cup points system are like unicorns — they don’t exist. Thankfully, golf fans who understand the future PGA Tour points system should be considerably more common.

That’s because the new system will be fully standardized across every event. A win will mean the same 300 points on the Championship Series as on the Challenger Series, the Korn Ferry Tour, and the Fall Series.

Like the Championship Series, the Challenger Series will also feature a 90-player stroke play event to determine the season-long winner. Unlike the Championship Series, the Challenger’s season-long winner will earn a crazy incentive: the winner of the season-finale event earns a season-long promotion to the Championship Series no matter where he finishes on the points list.

title: Which LIV Golfers Have Joined The DP World Tour In 2027?
article_text:
There are exciting times ahead on the DP World Tour after 19 former LIV golfers were given routes into the European circuit's ecosystem ahead of the 2027 campaign.

The most high-profile name among them belongs to Bryson DeChambeau, who had previously indicated he was set on committing to the latest edition of LIV Golf before the team-based league was forced into liquidation.

However, with very few options left on the table due to the PGA Tour failing to offer any kind of fresh olive branch, DeChambeau submitted the necessary paperwork to become a DP World Tour member just hours before Sunday's deadline.

The two-time Major winner will take up Category 1 status on the DP World Tour, earned due to winning the US Open in both 2022 and 2024.

Other ex-LIV pros in the same category - which allows for unrestricted access to any DP World Tour event next term - include Sergio Garcia, Henrik Stenson, Martin Kaymer, Graeme McDowell, Louis Oosthuizen and Charl Schwartzel.

Nine more players who have previously plied their trade with the LIV Golf League have signed agreements to receive invites to "a specific number of tournaments" next season, but not before the Bahrain Championship in late January.

Those invites will also not include Rolex Series events, with designated events for each player where their presence will "add value to those tournaments," per the DP World Tour.

Subscribe to the Golf Monthly newsletter to stay up to date with all the latest tour news, equipment news, reviews, head-to-heads and buyer’s guides from our team of experienced experts.

The European circuit went on to say the structure of the invites has been carefully considered in order to "ensure and preserve playing opportunities for existing members."

Dustin Johnson, Cameron Smith and Bubba Watson are the three Major champions to have signed that deal while Abraham Ancer, Lucas Herbert, Michael La Sasso, Joaquin Niemann, Carlos Ortiz and Thomas Pieters are among the other pros hoping to make the most of their opportunities.

In a statement, DP World Tour CEO Guy Kinnings said: “There has been significant change in the landscape of men’s professional golf over the past 12 months.

"As golf’s global tour, we have taken a pragmatic approach to this unique and unprecedented situation as we go into next year, always with the best interests of our entire membership at the forefront of our minds.

“We realise there are different viewpoints but this approach, discussed and agreed with our Tournament Committee and allied to this responsibly managed programme of invites, will add value which, in turn, will benefit the tour as a whole.

“We therefore look forward to beginning our 2027 season at the BMW Australian PGA Championship next week, a season where our fans will enjoy enhanced and competitive fields at our historic tournaments around the world.”

While 19 players are moving home tours, at least 31 players who appeared in a LIV Golf event last term are expected to tee it up on the European circuit next year.

Jon Rahm confirmed he was leaving LIV Golf last month and has since wrapped up his status beyond doubt by winning the Abu Dhabi Championship. The same is true for Tyrrell Hatton after triumphing at the DP World Tour Championship.

Thomas Detry, David Puig, Branden Grace and Elvis Smylie are among LIV's other more successful names make their DP World Tour return once the new campaign starts down in Australia next week.

Jose Luis Ballester, Byeong Hun An and John Catlin are among the former LIV names to have earned their way back via Q-School recently.

Jonny Leighfield is our Staff News Writer who joined Golf Monthly just in time for the 2023 Solheim Cup and Ryder Cup. He graduated from the University of Brighton with a degree in Sport Journalism in 2017 and spent almost five years as the sole sports reporter at his local newspaper. During his time with Golf Monthly, Jonny has interviewed several stars of the game, including Robert MacIntyre, Ian Poulter, Lee Westwood, and Joaquin Niemann. An improving golfer himself, Jonny enjoys learning as much about the game as he can and recently reached his Handicap goal of 18 for the first time.

title: Over 30 Ex-LIV Golfers Will Play On The DP World Tour Next Year - But What About The Others?
article_text:
The DP World Tour is set to be the golf tour to watch in 2027 following LIV Golf's collapse, with the likes of Jon Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau and many more of the former Saudi-backed tour's star names solely competing on the European Tour next year.

DeChambeau has joined as a 'Category 1' member as a recent Major winner, while many other big names have either earned status, rejoined or agreed sponsor invitation deals.

Cameron Smith, Joaquin Niemann and Dustin Johnson are three of nine men to have agreed to a number of sponsor's invitations for certain events, while Ryder Cup legends Sergio Garcia, Lee Westwood and Ian Poulter have also rejoined.

So that is 31 of the 67 accounted for, but what about the other 36?

Based on the 2026 individual standings, Anthony Kim is currently LIV's best player who does not have tour status next year.

The three-time PGA Tour winner, who returned to professional golf after 12 years in 2024, produced one of the best stories in the sport this year when he won his first title since 2010 at LIV Golf Adelaide. He went on to finish 7th in the individual standings.

Kim recently stated he "knows" an "opportunity's coming" and vowed to keep his game in-shape. The enigmatic American may well receive sponsor's invitations into DP World Tour and Asian Tour events next season as he continues his comeback.

LIV's second-highest finisher who will not be playing on the DP World Tour is Scott Vincent. The Zimbabwean placed 10th in the LIV Golf League, and he will likely continue to ply his trade in Asia.

Vincent, who I ranked as one of LIV's top 10 players this summer, has three Japan Golf Tour titles as well as two Asian Tour victories.

Many other ex-LIV full-time players and reserves should also take the Asian Tour route, with the likes of Peter Uihlein, Richard T Lee, Younghan Song, Yosuke Asaji, Ben Campbell, Miguel Tabuena, Minkyu Kim, Travis Smyth, Wade Ormsby, Jeongwoo Ham, Ollie Schniederjans and Cameron John all card-holders.

Anirban Lahiri may well continue playing in Asia without any DP World Tour status, while another veteran Richard Bland will almost certainly mix the Legends Tour with senior Majors.

There had been some recent controversial talk of Charles Howell III cutting a deal with the DP World Tour, but he was not named as one of the nine players to agree to 'receive invites to a specific number of tournaments next season.'

The 47-year-old veteran, who has made over 600 PGA Tour starts, may just wait out his PGA Tour suspension before trying to progress back through the Korn Ferry Tour.

Dean Burmester is another big name who has no DP World Tour status next year, but he will likely find himself in the South African co-sanctioned events and continue to play on the Sunshine Tour.

The future is currently unknown for a number of LIV's Americans, like Harold Varner III, Talor Gooch, Matthew Wolff, Brendan Steele, Cameron Tringale and Jason Kokrak.

It is the same for PGA Tour winners Marc Leishman, Danny Lee and Sebastian Munoz.

Every LIV Golfer is currently serving a 12-month suspension from the PGA Tour, so these names, as suggested with Howell, may opt to wait it out before attempting to work their way back up. They're all big names of varying degrees so could be seen in tour events in regions like Asia and Australasia.

Caleb Surratt and Luis Masaveu have HotelPlanner Tour status and both have the talent to progress to the main tour fairly quickly. It may be that a few other ex-LIV pros find their way to the DP World Tour feeder circuit at some point in 2027, too.

Sam Horsfield is another man who currently doesn't appear to have tour status anywhere, either. The three-time DP World Tour winner may well receive invites into Asian Tour or HotelPlanner Tour events but that is just speculation at the moment.

And finally, it would be remise not to mention Phil Mickelson. The six-time Major champion and golfing legend was highly influential in LIV Golf's controversial launch, and where he goes next from here remains to be seen.

Lefty has lifetime exemptions into The Masters and PGA Championship and is also eligible for senior Majors. He has had some high-profile personal issues this year and has only played in one tournament, so it is currently unknown when, or even if, we'll see him tee it up again.

There are certainly plenty of LIV Golfers who have come out of the league's collapse as winners, with tens of millions in their bank accounts while being able to walk back onto tours with full status.

For some, however, it is a different story as they find themselves at a crossroad in their careers.

How things shake out as players get back into the traditional ecosystem and work their way back up will make for many fascinating storylines.

LIV Golf fractured the men's game like never seen before back in 2022, and next year will make for a very entertaining campaign at the sport begins to heal and come back together.

Elliott Heath, our Engagement Editor, has been with Golf Monthly since early 2016 after graduating with a degree in Sports Journalism. He covered the 2022 and 2025 Masters from Augusta National and was there by the 18th green to watch Rory McIlroy complete the career grand slam. He has also covered six Open Championships on-site including the 150th at St Andrews. He has played golf for almost his entire life and holds a handicap of six.

title: "No winners" - Paul McGinley speaks out after LIV Golf stars handed major lifeline
article_text:
Former European Ryder Cup captain Paul McGinley says "there are no winners in this whole scenario" after Bryson DeChambeau and several LIV Golf players secured places on the DP World Tour for the 2027 season.

American DeChambeau, 33, was among the first wave of players to quit the PGA Tour for the breakaway league in 2022.

He remained committed to LIV despite Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrawing its multi-billion-dollar financial support, but faced an uncertain future after the league confirmed it would wind down operations.

There was speculation DeChambeau, who claimed he "tried everything" to save LIV, would spend the next 12 months focusing on his YouTube and social media channels alongside playing in the four men's majors before possibly attempting to return to the PGA Tour.

But the two-time U.S. Open champion ended the speculation surrounding his competitive future on Tuesday after taking up category one membership on the DP World Tour.

Telegraph Sport reported DeChambeau submitted his papers on Sunday, hours before the deadline.

Other major champions, including Dustin Johnson, Cameron Smith and Bubba Watson, have signed agreements to receive invitations to a specific number of tournaments next season.

There will also be returns for European Tour veterans such as Ian Poulter, Lee Westwood, Paul Casey, Graeme McDowell and Sergio Garcia.

That development will almost certainly raise eyebrows.

Poulter and Westwood left the circuit in acrimonious circumstances after taking their initial fines and suspensions to a sports arbitration panel.

After losing the case, they resigned their memberships in April 2023 and vowed never to pay any more fines beyond the initial £100,000 penalty.

Poulter said he believed the fines were unjust and didn't even want LIV's financiers to pay them on his behalf so he could continue his career on his home tour.

Westwood previously said: "I'm not paying them because I disagree with the way they've been handed out."

Veteran Dutch pro, Joost Luiten, told GolfMagic last month that it would be a "weak decision" to allow LIV players to easily walk back through the door and not head to qualifying school.

Luiten said his concern was that there would be fewer opportunities for emerging talents and those who "remained loyal".

Chief executive Guy Kinnings said the organisation had taken a "pragmatic approach" to a "unique and unprecedented situation".

McGinley told Sky Sports: "The guys I feel sorry for are the guys not so much next year in 2027 on the DP World Tour, it's 2028 because you've got 30 really world class players coming back to play on the DP World Tour next year from LIV.

"And they're probably going to take 20 or 30 of the 100 cards that are available. So there's really 20 or 30 less spots for the current players to play for next year in terms of keeping their status for 2028.

"So that's going to be a difficult scenario for them and they didn't get the riches that the guys went to LIV did. So I can understand why they're feeling aggrieved."

McGinley added: "There's no real winners in this whole scenario. There's not a clear cut winner in this scenario. It's been pretty ugly for golf in the last two or three years.

"And now it's time to put the pieces back together and starting next year having the LIV guys back playing in Europe is the start of trying to put this game back together and relationships back together."

title: Woods set to return next month after two years out
article_text:
Tiger Woods is set to return to competitive golf in December for the first time in more than two years.

Woods, 50, has not played in a traditional ranking event since the 2024 Open Championship at Royal Troon amid a series of off-course issues.

The 15-time major champion has endured a challenging few years with a number of injuries and turmoil in his personal life.

Woods will host next month's Hero World Challenge - an event which is part of the PGA Tour schedule but does not carry FedEx Cup points - and has been announced as part of the 20-player field.

The American is one of three exemptions for the tournament in the Bahamas along with compatriots Rickie Fowler and Gary Woodland.

Speaking to SiriusXM PGA Tour Radio in a video posted last week, Woods said: "I'm feeling better, no doubt about that.

"I've been training quite a bit. I will be at Hero either way, so I'll see you there."

Woods' long-awaited return comes after he accepted a five-year driving ban in September following a plea agreement in his reckless driving case.

In March, Woods had been arrested and charged with driving under the influence after clipping a truck and rolling his car in Florida.

Woods was also found with two white pills in his pocket, which were identified as hydrocodone - an opioid used to treat pain.

He subsequently stepped away from golf to seek treatment in what was described by his attorney as an "intensive, highly individualised and medically integrated programme".

Woods has endured a succession of debilitating injuries, including multiple back surgeries, serious fractures to his right leg following a car crash in 2021 and a ruptured Achilles tendon in 2025.

Woods also suffered the death of his mother, Kultida, in February 2025, while his girlfriend Vanessa Trump was diagnosed with breast cancer earlier this year.

Trump, the former daughter-in-law of US President Donald Trump, said last month that she is now cancer free.

title: Tiger Woods: 15-time major champion to make PGA Tour comeback at December's Hero World Challenge in Bahamas
article_text:
Tiger Woods has confirmed he will return to competitive action at the Hero World Challenge next month, live on Sky Sports.

The invite-only tournament - hosted by Woods' foundation - has previously been used as a comeback event for Woods, who has played a limited schedule since suffering career-threatening injuries in a car crash in February 2021.

Woods has not appeared on the PGA Tour since missing the cut at The Open in July 2024, with the 15-time major champion missing the entire 2025 season after rupturing his Achilles tendon.

He underwent fresh back surgery last October and missed the 2026 campaign after "stepping away" from PGA Tour golf, following a car crash in March that saw him charged with reckless driving, but is now scheduled to return in Albany, Bahamas.

The 50-year-old is one of three sponsor's exemptions added to the field for the 20-man event, held from December 3-6, with 2019 US Open champion Gary Woodland and Rickie Fowler the others to be included.

Woods was a notable absentee from the initial line-up announcement last month, with Hideki Matsuyama returning as defending champion and Scottie Scheffler looking to win for a third time in four years, while Players champion Cameron Young and former US Open winner Matt Fitzpatrick also feature.

The former world No 1 is currently listed as 'unranked' in the OWGR standings, having only completed four 72-hole tournaments over the last six seasons and not had a worldwide top 10 since January 2020.

He last featured at the Hero World Challenge in 2023, his first appearance since withdrawing mid-tournament from The Masters earlier that year, although won the event in 2001, 2004, 2006, 2007 and 2011.

Woods was listed in Jupiter Links GC's expanded five-player roster for the 2026/27 TGL season, beginning December 27, with Kevin Kisner - replaced by Keith Mitchell in the line-up - expecting the five-time Masters champion to feature more frequently.

"I'm not on the team anymore," Kisner told the Fore Play Podcast last month. "I had a two-year contract with Jupiter Links. Tiger wants to play and they wanted to sign Keith Mitchell, which is totally fine with me.

"Rob [McNamara], Tiger's guy, he texted me a long text last week. Just telling me what they did on their decisions, how they were moving around and what players were going to do and that Tiger wanted to play a full schedule."

Woods previously described the PNC Championship as his "fifth major", with the 36-hole team competition seeing a former winner of a major or The Players tee it up alongside a family member.

He featured in every edition since 2020 with his son, Charlie Woods, who fired a hole-in-one during the 2024 contest before they lost in a play-off to Bernhard Langer's team, although missed last year's contest due to injury.

Team Woods have yet to confirm their entry into this year's edition, held from December 19-20 and also live on Sky Sports, although there are spaces for them still to be included in the line-up.

"He plays there [at the Hero World Challenge] and PNC [Championship]," Kisner predicted. "He's going to play both.

"Come back, get your feet wet at the Hero, play with Charlie [Woods] in the Father/Son, play some TGL, get ready for Augusta."

title: DP World Tour chief executive explains why including ex-LIV Golf members in 2027 is 'huge opportunity' to strengthen events
article_text:
DP World Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings insists welcoming LIV Golfers back as part of their tournaments is a ‘huge opportunity’ to strengthen its events next season.

The DP World Tour announced last month they would prevent membership next season to players signing up to the proposed 'LIV 2.0', prior to the rival circuit's subsequent winding down of operations.

The deadline to confirm DP World Tour membership for the 2027 season ended on Sunday following the conclusion of the Race to Dubai campaign, with multiple LIV Golfers set to be more frequently involved over the coming year.

The decision to include some past LIV players has caused debate from current DP World Tour members, although Kinnings believes it can enhance tournaments during times when the golfing calendar is focused on the PGA Tour.

"We're going to assess [membership applications] and then we'll make an announcement on Tuesday about that," Kinnings exclusively told Sky Sports.

"For us, it's the prospect of having incredible talent joining our tour, which already is laden with talent.

"There's the top 100 that have kept their DP World Tour cards, 15 coming from HotelPlanner Tour, 20 from Tour School. Top players coming from all of our global partnerships - all of that together will lead to significantly stronger fields.

"What it does is it brings it [strength in fields] at the time of year when our dual members are off in the United States and that will help those [DP World Tour] tournaments at that time of year.

"That will make happy promoters, happy sponsors, happy broadcasters, hopefully happy fans. We see it as a huge opportunity and what it will be is at the right time and hopefully great strong fields throughout the year."

Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton are expected to play full-time on the DP World Tour in 2027, with golfers ineligible for 12 months on the PGA Tour from their previous LIV Golf start, while Bryson DeChambeau is yet to confirm whether he will accept membership as a recent major champion.

Golf Channel LA reported that Niemann would play "approximately 15 DP World Tour tournaments through wild cards, a number that could increase if he wins a title", having previous won nine times on LIV Golf.

Ex-LIV golfers Thomas Pieters, Michael La Sasso and Carlos Ortiz all have invites to the BMW Australian PGA Championship, the opening event of the new season, with deals reportedly expected to be agreed on how many DP World Tour starts players will get.

The PGA Tour is undergoing significant changes to its schedule from 2028, with a Championship Series and Challenger Series running concurrently, while discussions are ongoing to finalise the pathway - and how many cards - that will be available from the DP World Tour to the US-based tour.

"I think with the PGA Tour clearly planning from 2028 onwards to focus their tour in that February to August time, it gives us a chance to build and strengthen what we have in that time around the world," Kinnings added.

"It also give us the opportunity from the start of September to the end of January to really have the very strongest tournaments around the world. We can shine a light on international golf with some stunning fields.

"So, working together with them [PGA Tour], I think there's a huge opportunity for us both. We're in the middle of very positive conversations (with the PGA Tour). We're hoping to have news certainly by the New Year."

Rory McIlroy said earlier this month he hopes the men's professional game can now stabilise after a turbulent few years, with the world No 2 expecting ex-LIV Golf members to make his hopes of winning a record ninth Race to Dubai title in 2027 a tougher challenge.

"Next year [winning the Race to Dubai] is going to be tough because you've got the likes of Jon [Rahm] and Tyrrell [Hatton] and some of these guys coming back [from LIV Golf] and playing a full-time DP World Tour schedule," McIlroy explained in his press conference.

"Obviously I'll be sort of bouncing around a little bit on both the DP World Tour and the PGA Tour, so I think The Race to Dubai next year is going to be incredibly competitive.

"I reckon it's going to be a little more difficult [to win]. Not that it's not difficult every year, but even more difficult next year with those guys playing a full-time schedule over here. I'll just have to go out there and play well and accumulate points early.

"If I have to maybe Beef up my schedule at the end of next year to try to compete with them, if I'm in with a close enough chance of doing it, I'll do that."

title: DeChambeau joins DP World Tour after LIV Golf collapse
article_text:
Two-time US Open champion Bryson DeChambeau has agreed to join the DP World Tour for next season.

DeChambeau was among a host of star names who joined LIV Golf four years ago and maintained his commitment even after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew its financial backing for the breakaway tour in April.

Earlier this month the 33-year-old American said he "gave everything" to keep LIV Golf alive as the tour confirmed its intention to wind down operations.

As first reported in the Telegraph,, external DeChambeau successfully submitted his application to join the European Tour before Sunday's deadline.

DeChambeau has already confirmed he will compete in Gary Player's Nedbank Golf Challenge - a DP World Tour event - in South Africa in December.

As a recent major champion DeChambeau has been given 'category one' membership by the DP World Tour, which means he is guaranteed entry to any event across the season.

Dustin Johnson, Cameron Smith and Bubba Watson - other former major champions who defected to LIV - have signed agreements to receive invitations to a specific number of tournaments.

Veteran English trio Ian Poulter, Lee Westwood and Paul Casey, plus Northern Ireland's Graeme McDowell, are among a number of ex-LIV players who are eligible to play on the DP World Tour in 2027.

The full-time return of Spain's Jon Rahm and England's Tyrrell Hatton, who did not resign their memberships, has also been confirmed.

"There has been significant change in the landscape of men's professional golf over the past 12 months," said DP World Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings.

"As golf's global tour, we have taken a pragmatic approach to this unique and unprecedented situation as we go into next year, always with the best interests of our entire membership at the forefront of our minds."

As one of the poster boys of LIV Golf, and one of the biggest names in the sport, it was intriguing to see what DeChambeau would do next.

With LIV golfers automatically banned for a year by the PGA Tour, it was thought he might decide to focus on his YouTube and social media channels - which have attracted a new, younger audience of many millions - over the next 12 months.

But joining the DP World Tour is a logical option for the big-hitting American, who reportedly received £95m, external to join LIV in 2022 and earned almost £50m in prize money over four seasons.

Signing up for the European-based tour means he can play the traditional format of the game on a regular basis and offers a pathway back to the PGA Tour.

The leading 10 players on the DP World Tour in a season are guaranteed PGA Tour cards for the following season, which was a route taken by Patrick Reed - DeChambeau's former US Ryder Cup team-mate - when he left LIV before the start of the 2026 season.

For the DP World Tour, DeChambeau brings further star power to their product.

DeChambeau will join the likes of European superstars Rory McIlroy and Tommy Fleetwood as full-time members, and boosts the tour's stock as the golfing landscape continues to realign following LIV's demise.

"I think a name like Bryson DeChambeau and everything he brings with him, good and bad, he brings eyeballs, which is a good thing for tournaments," McIlroy said earlier this month.

Six-time major champion McIlroy also claimed those connected to LIV were expressing an ambition to "destroy the European Tour" during this year's Masters.

Instead, the Saudi-backed venture is to be liquidated and has led to an influx of big-names joining the DP World Tour.

As well as DeChambeau being given membership for the first time, it was announced that Johnson, Smith and Watson are among a group of nine former LIV players allowed to play a limited number of events.

They will be picked at the discretion of the DP World Tour to "add value to those tournaments", which is designed to prevent full-time members from missing playing opportunities.

On allowing former LIV players to join the tour, Kinnings added: "We realise there are different viewpoints.

"But this approach, discussed and agreed with our tournament committee and allied to this responsibly managed programme of invites, will add value which, in turn, will benefit the tour as a whole."

title: DJ, Cam Smith, Bubba given DP World Tour lifeline. Here’s all the ex-LIV players who have European status
PGA Tour confirm 'no plans' for returning route for LIV Golf players as Tiger Woods backs big changes to tour's structure
article_text:
PGA Tour chief executive Brian Rolapp insists there are currently no plans to reintroduce a “Returning Member Program” to welcome back former LIV Golf players.

LIV Golf confirmed earlier this month they were winding down operations instead of launching a new version, because of a lack of financial support, leaving players looking for pathways back to traditional tours.

Brooks Koepka took financial penalties earlier this year to return to the PGA Tour via the Returning Member Program, a pathway created for a limited group of 'elite performers', with Bryson DeChambeau, Jon Rahm and Cameron Smith elected not to follow suit.

Rahm has said he 'probably would do it' if offered a similar route back again, while DeChambeau said he would go about 'whatever is next the right way' and has since accepted DP World Tour membership, although Rolapp has played down that - as things stand - being a possibility next season.

"There are no plans for that currently, no," Rolapp told reporters on a media call, following the PGA Tour approving details for its new competitive structure from 2028.

Players are currently suspended for 12 months from their last LIV Golf appearance before being eligible to feature on the PGA Tour, with Patrick Reed being a full-time member on the DP World Tour this season before heading back to the US circuit in 2027.

Sergio Garcia, Dustin Johnson and Joaquin Niemann are among the players following a similar schedule on the DP World Tour next season, with the PGA Tour having "thoughtful discussion" about how to incorporate LIV Golf players going forward.

"We have heard from our fans and we know that they want the best players playing together and we share that view," Rolapp added. "I have said that from day one when I took the job, I am interested in doing whatever makes the PGA Tour better.

"I have said that from day one when I took the job, I am interested in doing whatever makes the PGA Tour better. As we have a membership organization, we have rules and, as I shared before, they exist to ensure fairness and competitive balance.

"Rules matter and they will be enforced. We engaged in thoughtful discussion on the topic of LIV players with both boards [PGA Tour and the PGA Tour Enterprises]. As far as we have read, bankruptcy proceedings are ongoing and the process is complex.

"I hope to have more to say in the beginning of the New Year but, until that time, I will not speculate on the outcome or individual decisions players make."

The Future Competition Committee - chaired by Tiger Woods - announced Monday further details of the PGA Tour's new competitive structure, set to debut in 2028.

"I can confidently say the PGA Tour is in the best position it has ever been," Woods said. "We created a competitive model grounded in meritocracy, built to last and that offers the best opportunity for the next generation of players."

The PGA Tour is doing away with the PGA Tour Americas, instead creating a vast network of feeder tournaments throughout the year that will have one ranking system.

The Korn Ferry Tour will have at least 20 tournaments with $1m purses (£756,000) and the leading 20 players will be promoted to the Challenger Series.

The top 20 players in the Challenger Series advance to the Championship Series, with the board approving elevating the final event that would be for the top 90 players.

The winner of the season finale would be promoted to the Championship Series, even if he isn't among the top 20. The number of places on the Championship Series via the DP World Tour's "Race to Dubai" rankings has yet to be finalised.

title: Nine more LIV Golf players follow Bryson DeChambeau to DP World Tour
article_text:
A number of LIV Golf players are converging on the DP World Tour. These are the players with deals to play in Europe next season…

The DP World Tour will capitalise on the PGA Tour’s one-year suspension facing former LIV Golf players by offering the ‘homeless’ stars a pathway back to European golf in 2027.

After securing arguably the biggest coup by landing Bryson DeChambeau, the DP World Tour has further boosted its star power by agreeing deals with nine more former LIV Golf players.

DeChambeau’s situation is different to the other players, having secured Category One membership through his 2024 US Open victory. This gives him full playing privileges on the DP World Tour in 2027, rather than relying on any help from the Tour.

For the others, DP World Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings has introduced a new invitation programme to accommodate the unprecedented number of non-members seeking playing opportunities on golf’s traditional tours following LIV’s demise.

As first revealed by TG last month, a number of former LIV players who would otherwise have needed to progress through Q School or seek playing opportunities on the Asian Tour have been in talks with Wentworth officials over agreements guaranteeing them a set number of invitations to DP World Tour events.

It’s a sliding scale, with more invitations awarded to players perceived to bring greater value to the tour. However, none of those receiving these agreements will be eligible for the most lucrative Rolex Series tournaments.

The DP World Tour hopes the arrangements will strengthen fields at smaller tournaments that might otherwise lack star power.

The former LIV Golf players receiving these deals include major champions Dustin Johnson, Cameron Smith and Bubba Watson, who will feature on the DP World Tour in 2027 after agreeing to receive invitations to a specific number of tournaments next season.

They are among a group of nine players to have agreed such arrangements, alongside Abraham Ancer, Lucas Herbert, Michael La Sasso, Joaquin Niemann, Carlos Ortiz and Thomas Pieters.

The allocation of invitations across the season has been carefully managed by the Tour’s Player Relations Department, following extensive modelling to ensure playing opportunities for existing members are protected.

Guy Kinnings, the DP World Tour’s Chief Executive, said: “Following the success of our 2026 season, in which three of our members won Major Championships and our players regularly showcased their talent on the global stage, our 2027 season is set to be one of the most keenly contested campaigns in our 55-year history.

“There has been significant change in the landscape of men’s professional golf over the past 12 months. As golf’s global Tour, we have taken a pragmatic approach to this unique and unprecedented situation as we go into next year, always with the best interests of our entire membership at the forefront of our minds.

“We realise there are different viewpoints but this approach, discussed and agreed with our Tournament Committee and allied to this responsibly managed programme of invites, will add value which, in turn, will benefit the Tour as a whole.

“We therefore look forward to beginning our 2027 season at the BMW Australian PGA Championship next week, a season where our fans will enjoy enhanced and competitive fields at our historic tournaments around the world.”

The arrangements represent a significant opportunity for the DP World Tour to strengthen its fields at a time when many of its biggest names are competing on the PGA Tour. They also provide a lifeline for players who would otherwise have faced a difficult route back into top-level professional golf, although the decision to offer invitations rather than require them to earn their way back through Q School is unlikely to please everyone among the tour’s existing membership.

Whatever your view on whether players who joined LIV Golf should be afforded such an easy route back, the 2027 DP World Tour season looks like one for the ages.

title: Membership categories set for 2027 DP World Tour season
article_text:
The Membership Categories for the 2027 DP World Tour season have been finalised following the conclusion of the 2026 Race to Dubai on Sunday.

In total 199 players from 29 different countries will be exempt in Categories 1-18 to compete in 2027.

The addition of Bryson DeChambeau joining as a member for the first time in Category 1 takes the total of Major Champions in exempt membership to 22 for the 2027 season. He joins Rory McIlroy, Ryan Fox, Aaron Rai, Matt Fitzpatrick, Justin Thomas, Jon Rahm, Patrick Reed, J.J. Spaun, Shane Lowry, Justin Rose, Adam Scott, Francesco Molinari, Sergio Garcia, Henrik Stenson, Pádraig Harrington, Retief Goosen, Martin Kaymer, Graeme McDowell, Louis Oosthuizen, Danny Willett and Charl Schwartzel.

For a full list of exempt members and categories click here.

Furthermore, Major Champions Dustin Johnson, Cameron Smith and Bubba Watson will also feature on the DP World Tour in 2027 having signed agreements to receive invites to a specific number of tournaments next season.

They are among a group of nine players to sign such agreements, along with Abraham Ancer, Lucas Herbert, Michael La Sasso, Joaquin Niemann, Carlos Ortiz and Thomas Pieters.

The agreements relate to events on the DP World Tour and will be in effect from the Bapco Energies Bahrain Championship onwards during the 2027 season. They relate to specific tournaments, excluding those in the Rolex Series, and include designated events for each player which were prescribed by the DP World Tour to add value to those tournaments. The inventory of invites across the season has been carefully managed by the Tour’s Player Relations Department, following extensive modelling to ensure and preserve playing opportunities for existing members.

Guy Kinnings, the DP World Tour’s Chief Executive, said: “Following the success of our 2026 season, in which three of our members won Major Championships and our players regularly showcased their talent on the global stage, our 2027 season is set to be one of the most keenly contested campaigns in our 55-year history.

“There has been significant change in the landscape of men’s professional golf over the past 12 months. As golf’s global Tour, we have taken a pragmatic approach to this unique and unprecedented situation as we go into next year, always with the best interests of our entire membership at the forefront of our minds.

“We realise there are different viewpoints but this approach, discussed and agreed with our Tournament Committee and allied to this responsibly managed programme of invites, will add value which, in turn, will benefit the Tour as a whole.

“We therefore look forward to beginning our 2027 season at the BMW Australian PGA Championship next week, a season where our fans will enjoy enhanced and competitive fields at our historic tournaments around the world.”
